prompts.L3:

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker explores a monotonous, terror-filled night through surreal imagery, jazz-like repetition, and contradictions that evoke claustrophobia and unseen danger. Despite a world choked by warnings, pollution, and personal threats, the speaker remains alive inside the damaged building, making survival itself the poem’s defiant conclusion.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: this little phase

outputs.L1:
This little phase continues in the same way, without variety: jazz and compromise making blue snow grow at the windows; mohair fumes clogging my throat like cats; flames pouncing without burning; shadows gathering in parkas at my back.

Turn so I can see your face. Stand where I can see you, man.

Should someone phone, I will tell whoever it is that I cannot escape this night. Even saxophones do not dry-light the brown sweat, the terror in white doorways beneath multicolored covers. There is no way to sleep with the phone falling off the hook, with the blaring beep of warnings:

Do not leave your house.  
Do not stay home.

This is the contradiction of when I live. Even fanfares and flourishes do not announce a truce with our personal assailants. Without variety: blue dust, blood traces in floor wax, black fog, and nappy lint. Colorless wax spreads broad tears across all the windows.

Some permanent weather happened to this building. Some misplaced coal mine had its disaster here, and I am alive inside.
outputs.L2:
This brief stretch continues unchanged, stripped of variation. Jazz and concession coax blue snow to rise against the panes. Mohair smoke chokes me like a throatful of cats, while flames leap without scorching. Behind me, shadows bundled in parkas assemble. Turn around; let me look at your face. Stand within my sight, man.

If the telephone rings, I will tell whoever is calling that there is no escape from this night. Not even saxophones can dry or illuminate the brown, sweating fear lodged in white doorways beneath brightly colored blankets. Sleep is impossible: the receiver slips from its cradle, and an alarm shrieks conflicting orders—do not go outside; do not remain at home. Such is the paradox of the time in which I live.

No ceremonial brass or decorative flourish declares a ceasefire with the attackers assigned to each of us. Everything remains monotonous: blue powder, streaks of blood embedded in floor polish, black mist, and lint from tightly curled hair. Pale, colorless wax stretches wide tears over every window. Some lasting climate has overtaken this building, as though a coal mine wandered here and suffered its catastrophe. And inside it, I am still alive.
outputs.L3:
Life continues in a monotonous cycle, shaped by the muted rhythms of jazz, uneasy compromise, and a surreal atmosphere of oppression. Smoke drifts through the scene as shadows deepen, flames flicker, and darkened windows conceal whatever may be waiting beyond them. Together, these images create a powerful sense of suffocation and fear, suggesting the presence of a threat that cannot be clearly seen or understood.

Within this inescapable night, the speaker longs to see another person clearly, perhaps searching for reassurance, connection, or proof that they are not alone. Yet every attempt at clarity is frustrated by darkness and uncertainty. Contradictory warnings—one urging the speaker to leave the house, another insisting that they remain inside—only intensify the anxiety. Caught between escape and confinement, the speaker is unable to feel safe or find rest.

The building itself seems permanently marked by disaster, as though fire, violence, or some other catastrophe has left an irreversible scar upon it. Nevertheless, the speaker remains alive within its damaged walls. This survival offers no simple sense of relief; instead, it reinforces the disturbing tension between endurance and entrapment. Life continues, but it does so under the weight of fear, memory, and an atmosphere from which there appears to be no escape.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a night that feels both endless and terrifying, transforming ordinary experience into a surreal landscape of confinement and danger. Through dreamlike images, jazz-like rhythms, and repeated phrases, the speaker creates an atmosphere of monotony interrupted by sudden threats. Contradictions blur the boundary between safety and violence, suggesting that nothing can be trusted: the building may offer shelter, but it is also damaged and claustrophobic; the darkness may conceal the speaker, but it also hides whatever is approaching. The poem’s repetitive structure reinforces the sense of being trapped in a cycle, as though the speaker is reliving the same fear without any clear possibility of escape.

Beyond the immediate setting, the outside world appears contaminated by warnings, pollution, and both public and personal forms of danger. Environmental decay merges with psychological distress, making it difficult to separate real threats from imagined ones. The unseen nature of the danger intensifies the terror, since the speaker can sense its presence without fully identifying or confronting it. Yet the poem does not end in defeat. The speaker remains alive within the ruined building, and that continued existence becomes a quiet but forceful act of resistance. In a world defined by damage, suffocation, and fear, survival itself is the poem’s final defiant statement.
outputs.L5:
**This Little Phase**

They call it *this little phase* as if it will pass quietly—like rain tapping against the window or a song forgotten by morning. Maybe they are right. Maybe one day the clothes, the music, the late-night thoughts, and the sudden need to become someone new will feel like pieces of another life.

But right now, this little phase is everything.

It is the courage to ask questions no one else wants to answer. It is changing direction without knowing where the road leads. It is making mistakes, growing out of old dreams, and discovering that becoming yourself is rarely graceful.

Perhaps every life is made of little phases: brief seasons that seem permanent while we are living them. They shape us, soften us, and leave something behind.

So let this little phase be strange, bright, difficult, and honest. Let it take the time it needs. Even if it passes, it will have mattered.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in all lowercase about urban claustrophobia, winter, jazz, ringing phones, and the feeling of being trapped inside a contaminated building.
counterfactuals.output:
winter has rented every room in the city and nailed the windows shut. outside, the avenues fold into gray accordions, squeezing buses, pigeons, and small exhausted gods between their pleats. inside this building, the radiators cough up a yellow heat that tastes of pennies. warning tape blooms along the stairwells. the elevator opens on floors that do not exist.

somewhere behind the walls, a saxophone worries the same blue sentence until it frays. the notes crawl through the vents wearing little masks. they settle on our tongues like ash.

every phone begins ringing at once.

we answer, but there is only snow breathing on the line. we hang up, and the bells continue inside our bones. room 6b calls room 6b. the lobby calls the roof. the dead pay phone in the basement calls my childhood and asks to speak with whoever survived.

no one is permitted to leave. the doors have been sealed with red wax, government paper, and the thick fingerprints of fear. something invisible has entered the water. something patient is counting us through the pipes. we sleep in our coats beneath flickering lights while the city presses its enormous frozen face against the glass.

at midnight, the jazz becomes frantic. drums tumble down the emergency stairs. a trumpet shatters into bright insects. the bass walks in circles, looking for an exit.

i put my ear to the wall and hear the neighboring buildings whispering that they, too, are contaminated, that the whole city is one locked room, that winter is the key turning slowly in the sky.

then the phone rings again.

this time, it is my own voice asking from very far away: are you still inside?

i look at the sealed door, the sweating ceiling, the snow piling upward past the windows.

yes, i say.

but the line has already gone cold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a stream-of-consciousness poem with no punctuation, using images of blue snow, saxophones, shadows in parkas, black fog, and an unanswered telephone.
counterfactuals.output:
blue snow drifts through the rooms of morning  
and saxophones bloom in the stairwell  
golden throats calling down empty floors  

shadows in parkas cross the frozen river  
carrying pockets full of midnight  
while black fog gathers beneath the bridges  
soft as a secret forgetting its name  

somewhere an unanswered telephone rings  
and rings inside a house with no windows  
I follow the sound through blue snow  
past the saxophones breathing alone  
past every shadow turning away  

until even the black fog listens  
until the silence lifts the receiver  
and says nothing  
and keeps saying nothing
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental Beat-style monologue in which the speaker endures a night of contradictory emergency warnings and imagines the apartment building as the site of a coal-mine disaster.
counterfactuals.output:
At 2:13 the telephone screamed TORNADO and the television whispered STAY CALM while the radio, holy tin prophet on the windowsill, announced FLOODING IN LOW AREAS, though we lived on the ninth floor and the rain had forgotten to fall.

Then the sirens began arguing in the street.

Evacuate, said the red light.

Shelter in place, said the blue.

Do not use the elevators, said the elevator, opening its silver mouth on every floor.

I stood in my kitchen wearing one shoe, holding a wet towel over my face against smoke nobody could smell. The building groaned through its pipes, and suddenly it wasn’t a building anymore—it was Number Nine Colliery, sunk straight down through the black geology of midnight, every apartment a drift, every hallway a seam, every tenant a miner buried beneath ten thousand tons of rent, plaster, insomnia.

Mrs. Alvarez in 8B hammered the wall: three knocks, pause, three knocks.

Alive, alive, alive.

Old Leon from 6A shouted that the stairwell was on fire. A child shouted that the basement was underwater. Somebody shouted not to shout. Above us, boots stamped toward the roof; below us, boots stamped toward the lobby. The whole human mine moved in opposite directions.

My phone flashed:

SEEK HIGHER GROUND.

Then:

MOVE TO THE LOWEST INTERIOR ROOM.

Then:

THIS IS ONLY A TEST.

Then:

IMMEDIATE THREAT TO LIFE.

And I laughed—not because it was funny, no, but because laughter was the last canary we had, fluttering yellow and insane inside the rib cage.

I imagined the superintendent in a hard hat descending by cable, carrying a lamp and the master key. I imagined rescue crews drilling through the moon. I imagined reporters aboveground mispronouncing our names while we crouched in our furnished shafts with our unpaid bills, our canned beans, our family photographs shining like little fossils.

The ventilation fan coughed.

The lights died.

In the dark, the building became honest.

We heard every private terror: the dog scratching at 4C, the radiator praying, the newborn wailing two tunnels over. We heard the deep stone settle around us. We heard the city’s buried machinery chewing coal made of hours, coal made of wages, coal made of all the black mornings we had swallowed to keep the metropolis warm.

“Is it gas?” someone asked.

“Is it weather?”

“Is it war?”

No answer, only another alert vibrating in fifty pockets at once, a swarm of mechanical insects announcing:

DO NOT PANIC.

So naturally we panicked beautifully.

We dragged mattresses into bathtubs. We filled suitcases with water. We wrapped cats in blankets and documents in plastic. We confessed small crimes through locked doors. Leon admitted he’d been stealing everyone’s newspaper since 1997. Mrs. Alvarez forgave him, then took it back when another siren rose.

At 4:40, the emergency voice said the danger had passed.

At 4:41, the emergency voice said the danger was approaching.

At 4:42, the emergency voice became silence.

And silence was worst, because silence was the mine after the blast, when the dust hangs thick as judgment and each trapped soul presses an ear to the wall, waiting for the faint iron music of picks coming closer.

I put my palm against the plaster.

From the other side, another palm found mine.

No names. No instructions. No experts. Just heat through gypsum: proof of a body, proof of a tunnel, proof that the earth had not finished with us.

By dawn, nothing had happened and everything had happened.

The elevators resumed their ascent. The lobby filled with pale survivors carrying coffee cups, laundry baskets, bicycle helmets, birds in cages. We stepped into morning like miners hauled from a collapse, blinking at the indecent sky.

The city issued no apology.

The building stood black against the sunrise, all windows burning gold, and for one delirious second I saw us beneath the surface still—each in our narrow chamber, tapping our code into the walls:

Alive.

Alive.

Alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, hallucinatory prose poem about insomnia and fear in the city. Include strange sensory details, threats that remain unseen, references to jazz, and the closing realization that the narrator is still alive inside.
counterfactuals.output:
At 3:17 the city forgets its own name.

Streetlamps sweat a yellow syrup. Elevators breathe behind locked doors. Somewhere, a faucet counts backward in a language made of teeth. I lie awake while the ceiling lowers itself, inch by patient inch, carrying the faint odor of burnt violets.

Outside, tires whisper over wet asphalt. No cars pass.

From the apartment below comes a jazz trumpet—one blue note bent until it limps, then drums like knuckles testing a coffin lid. The bass walks alone through the walls. It stops whenever I stop breathing.

Something moves along the fire escape without weight. Something stands beneath my window, too tall for its shadow. I hear its coat brushing the bricks, though there is no wind, no coat, no one I can see.

The city glows under its skin: pharmacies, tunnels, all-night diners where spoons tremble in empty cups. Sirens bloom and rot in the distance. Every alley keeps its mouth open. Every darkened window watches with the same blind eye.

Toward dawn, the trumpet dissolves into static. The unseen thing withdraws—or enters. My heart kicks once against the black, then again.

And I understand, with fear and wonder, that I am still alive inside.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense free-verse passage that repeats the phrase “without variety” and blends domestic imagery—windows, floor wax, lint, covers, a phone off the hook—with apocalyptic weather and personal danger.
counterfactuals.output:
Without variety, the windows tremble in their putty,  
each pane holding the same bruised afternoon,  
the same black weather shouldering the roofs.

Without variety, I polish the floor wax  
into a small, obedient moon,  
while thunder drags its furniture upstairs  
and the gutters choke on leaves, feathers, ash.

Lint gathers beneath the radiators—  
gray nations, soft ruins—  
and the covers rise and fall on the bed  
as if something underneath has learned my breathing.

Without variety, the sirens circle.  
Without variety, the sky unfastens  
its red buttons, one by one.  
Rain comes down smelling of wire and scorched fields;  
hail mouths the windows; the house  
leans into its own terrified joints.

The phone is off the hook,  
swinging slightly above the floor,  
a dark fruit cut from every voice.  
I hear no warning, only the blunt pulse  
of someone at the door, or debris,  
or my heart rehearsing the intruder.

Without variety, the lights fail.  
Without variety, the hallway lengthens.  
I move through rooms slick with wax,  
my socks collecting lint, glass, the pale threads  
of everything we meant to keep covered.

Outside, the wind removes the neighborhood—  
fence, mailbox, tree, name—  
and lightning opens the world  
like a cupboard full of knives.

Without variety, I lock what will not hold.  
Without variety, I call what will not answer.  
The receiver breathes against the floorboards;  
the covers crawl toward the doorway;  
the windows fill with a single white fire—

and in that instant, without variety,  
every ordinary thing becomes a weapon,  
every shelter becomes a mouth,  
and I am still inside it, listening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
